GEN.1.1: This is the very first line of the Bible, spoken by the narrator before any person exists to hear it.
GEN.1.3: Still in the creation account, the narrator describes God speaking light into existence on the first day.
GEN.1.27: Continuing the creation account, the narrator describes God making the first humans, male and female.
GEN.2.24: The narrator pauses right after the first woman is created to explain why a man and woman become one family through marriage.
GEN.9.13: After the flood story ends, God speaks to Noah and his family, giving them a sign that he will never flood the whole earth again.
GEN.15.6: The narrator describes Abram's response after God promised him more descendants than he could count, though he had none yet.
GEN.28.15: Fleeing his brother's anger, Jacob is alone at night when God speaks to him in a dream, promising to bring him home safely.
GEN.50.20: Years after his brothers sold him into slavery, Joseph, now a powerful official in Egypt, reassures them that he holds no grudge.
EXO.3.14: Moses, tending sheep in the desert, asks a voice from a burning bush what name he should give the people of Israel.
EXO.14.14: Trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's army, Moses tells the terrified Israelites not to fight but to stay calm.
EXO.20.3: This is the first of the Ten Commandments, given to Moses on Mount Sinai for the people of Israel.
EXO.20.12: Part of the Ten Commandments Moses received on Mount Sinai, this one concerns how children should treat their parents.
EXO.20.13: One of the Ten Commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai, a short, direct rule against killing.
EXO.33.14: After the people had angered God by worshipping an idol, Moses asks for reassurance, and God answers him directly.
LEV.19.18: Part of a long list of laws Moses gave Israel, this one tells people how to treat their neighbors instead of holding grudges.
NUM.6.24: God gives Moses these exact words for the priests Aaron and his sons to say over the people of Israel.
NUM.23.19: Hired by a hostile king to curse Israel, the prophet Balaam instead speaks a blessing he says came from God.
DEU.4.29: Near the end of his life, Moses reminds the Israelites what will happen if they turn back to God after going astray.
DEU.30.19: In his final speech before the people cross into the new land without him, Moses lays out a choice between two paths.
JOS.1.9: After Moses's death, God speaks directly to Joshua, his successor, as he prepares to lead Israel into the new land.
JOS.24.15: Near the end of his life, Joshua gathers the tribes of Israel and challenges them to decide who they will serve.
RUT.1.16: A widow from Moab, Ruth refuses to leave her mother-in-law Naomi and go back to her own people.
1SA.3.10: A boy serving in the temple, Samuel hears a voice calling his name at night and, guided by the old priest Eli, answers it.
1SA.16.7: Sent to anoint Israel's next king, the prophet Samuel is about to pick Jesse's oldest son by his looks when God stops him.
1SA.30.6: Dismissed by the Philistines before any battle, David arrives home to find his camp burned and family taken, his men talking of stoning him.
1KI.18.21: On Mount Carmel, the prophet Elijah confronts a crowd of Israelites who have been worshipping both God and the god Baal.
1KI.19.12: Hiding in a cave after fleeing a death threat, Elijah waits through wind, an earthquake, and fire for God to speak.
2KI.6.16: Surrounded by an enemy army, Elisha's frightened servant is told not to be afraid, since more is on their side than he can see.
1CH.4.10: In a long list of family names, the narrator pauses to record a prayer from a man named Jabez, asking God to bless and protect him.
1CH.16.11: In a song David wrote for the priests to sing when Israel's sacred ark arrived in Jerusalem, worshippers are urged to seek God.
2CH.7.14: After Solomon finishes building the temple, God appears to him at night with a promise about what happens when the nation turns back after wrong.
2CH.20.15: Facing a massive invading army, King Jehoshaphat and the people of Judah hear a prophet named Jahaziel tell them not to be afraid.
NEH.8.10: After exiles returning to Jerusalem hear the law read aloud and weep, the leader Nehemiah tells them to celebrate instead.
EST.4.14: Esther's cousin Mordecai sends her this message, urging her to risk approaching the king to save her people from destruction.
JOB.1.21: After losing his children and property in a single day, Job tears his clothes, falls to the ground, and speaks these words.
JOB.2.10: After Job is struck with painful sores, his wife tells him to curse God and die, and this is his reply to her.
JOB.13.15: In the middle of arguing with friends who insist his suffering must be punishment, Job insists he will keep trusting God anyway.
JOB.14.1: In a long speech about the shortness and hardship of life, Job describes the human condition in general terms.
JOB.19.25: Despite his friends' accusations and his own suffering, Job insists to them that he still has someone who will defend him in the end.
JOB.23.10: Still defending himself to his friends, Job says that even though he cannot find God, God knows exactly what Job is going through.
JOB.38.4: After Job's long complaint and his friends' failed arguments, God finally speaks to Job out of a storm, questioning him directly.
JOB.42.5: Near the end of the book, after God has questioned him at length, Job replies, describing how his understanding of God has changed.
PSA.1.1: This opens the book of Psalms, describing the kind of person who avoids bad influences and finds happiness elsewhere.
PSA.1.3: Still in the opening psalm, the writer compares a person who follows good guidance to a tree planted by a river.
PSA.4.8: David wrote this short evening psalm, a simple statement of trust before going to sleep.
PSA.8.4: Looking up at the night sky, David wonders aloud in this psalm why God would bother paying attention to human beings at all.
PSA.9.10: In a psalm of praise, David reassures the reader that people who truly know God will trust him.
PSA.10.1: This psalm opens with the writer asking God directly why he feels distant during hard times.
PSA.16.11: In a psalm about trusting God even in death, David ends by describing lasting joy in God's presence.
PSA.18.2: David wrote this psalm after God rescued him from his enemies, including King Saul, who had hunted him for years.
PSA.19.1: Looking up at the sky, David describes in this psalm how creation itself seems to announce God's greatness without saying a word.
PSA.19.14: At the close of the same psalm about creation, David turns his praise into a personal prayer about his own words and thoughts.
PSA.22.1: David wrote this cry of anguish; centuries later, the Gospels record Jesus quoting these same opening words while dying on the cross.
PSA.23.1: David, who had worked as a shepherd before becoming king, opens this well-known psalm by picturing God in that same role.
PSA.23.2: Continuing the shepherd imagery of the same psalm, David describes the rest and care that image brings to mind.
PSA.23.3: Still using the shepherd image, David describes being guided along the right way.
PSA.23.4: The shepherd image turns darker here, as David pictures walking through a valley of deep shadow without fear.
PSA.23.5: Shifting from shepherd to host, David pictures God preparing a feast for him even while enemies look on.
PSA.23.6: This closes the psalm, with David expecting kindness to follow him for the rest of his life and beyond.
PSA.25.4: Trusting God rather than his own judgment, David opens this psalm by asking to be shown which way to go.
PSA.27.1: Facing enemies who wanted him dead, David opens this psalm by declaring where his confidence actually comes from.
PSA.27.14: David closes this psalm about facing hostile enemies by telling his own heart to keep waiting and stay brave.
PSA.28.7: In a psalm asking God not to stay silent, David shifts partway through to thanking God for already helping him.
PSA.29.11: This closes a psalm describing a violent storm as the voice of God, ending with a wish for peace over his people.
PSA.30.5: Written for the dedication of his house, David's psalm turns from sorrow to joy within a single verse.
PSA.32.8: After describing being forgiven, David reports God speaking directly to him, promising to guide and teach him.
PSA.34.8: Written after David pretended to be insane to escape a hostile king, this psalm invites the reader to test God's goodness personally.
PSA.34.17: The same psalm continues by describing God listening whenever people in trouble cry out for help.
PSA.34.18: Right after that, the same psalm adds that God stays close to anyone who is brokenhearted or crushed in spirit.
PSA.37.4: Advising against envy toward people who do wrong, David offers this alternative instead: finding joy in God himself.
PSA.37.5: David goes on immediately to say that handing his plans over to God is what makes them succeed.
PSA.37.23: By the end of this wisdom psalm, David describes a good life as something actively directed and steadied by God.
PSA.42.11: Talking to his own discouraged heart, the psalm's writer repeats this line as a refrain to talk himself back into hope.
PSA.46.1: Written by the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers, this psalm opens by naming God as a safe place during disaster.
PSA.46.10: Near the close of this psalm about disaster and refuge, God himself is quoted telling the nations to stop and take notice.
PSA.51.10: Written after the prophet Nathan confronted him over his affair with Bathsheba, David asks God for a fresh start.
PSA.55.22: Betrayed by a close friend, David tells himself in this psalm to hand his burden over to God and trust God to hold him up.
PSA.56.3: Written after the Philistines had captured him in the city of Gath, David admits his fear and where he takes it.
PSA.56.8: This same psalm, written while David was a captive, goes on to describe God keeping track of every tear he sheds.
PSA.61.2: Praying from somewhere far from home, David asks to be led to a place of safety higher than himself.
PSA.73.13: Written by Asaph, a temple musician, this verse voices his doubt after watching wicked people prosper while he suffers.
PSA.73.26: By the end of this psalm, Asaph's body may be failing, but he describes God as his strength regardless.
PSA.77.9: Wrestling with doubt, Asaph asks aloud in this psalm whether God has simply stopped being merciful.
PSA.84.10: Longing simply to be near God's temple, the sons of Korah compare one day there to a thousand anywhere else.
PSA.86.5: Calling himself poor and needy in this prayer, David describes God as quick to forgive and full of mercy.
PSA.88.14: One of the darkest psalms, this one written by Heman, a temple musician, asks God directly why he feels abandoned.
PSA.90.12: Reflecting on how short life is, the writer of this prayer attributed to Moses asks for wisdom about how to spend the time left.
PSA.91.1: With no named author, this psalm opens by describing the safety of a person who stays close to God.
PSA.91.2: A few lines into the same psalm, the writer responds with his own personal declaration of trust in God.
PSA.91.4: Using the image of a bird's sheltering feathers and wings, the same psalm describes God's protection as something close and constant.
PSA.91.11: This verse from the same psalm is later quoted by the devil while tempting Jesus in the wilderness, according to the Gospels.
PSA.95.2: Part of a call to worship with no named author, this verse invites the reader to come into God's presence giving thanks.
PSA.100.4: Labeled simply a psalm of praise with no named author, this verse instructs worshippers on how to enter the temple courts.
PSA.103.2: David tells his own soul not to forget anything good God has done for him, at the start of this psalm.
PSA.103.12: A few verses on, David uses the distance between east and west to describe how completely God forgives.
PSA.107.1: Opening a section of thanksgiving psalms with no named author, this verse calls on the reader to give thanks because God is good.
PSA.116.12: With no author named, the writer of this psalm asks what he can possibly give back to God for all he has received.
PSA.116.15: This thanksgiving psalm goes on to say that God values the lives of his faithful people even in their death.
PSA.118.24: Without a named author, this verse from a thanksgiving psalm celebrates the present day as something God himself made.
PSA.119.105: From the Bible's longest chapter, an alphabetic psalm with no named author, this verse compares God's word to a lamp for walking at night.
PSA.121.1: Part of a set of psalms called 'songs of ascents,' likely sung by travelers heading up to Jerusalem, this one asks where help truly comes from.
PSA.126.5: This 'song of ascents' compares hard work done through tears to a harvest that eventually comes in with joy.
PSA.133.1: David wrote this 'song of ascents,' celebrating the simple pleasure of family or community getting along peacefully.
PSA.139.7: In a psalm about being fully known by God, David asks whether there's anywhere at all he could go to escape that presence.
PSA.139.14: Continuing to reflect on how closely he was made and known, David praises God himself for crafting him so carefully.
PSA.139.23: Near the end of the same psalm, after admitting he hates his enemies, David asks God to search his own heart instead.
PSA.147.3: In a hymn praising God for rebuilding Jerusalem, this verse describes God's care for people who are grieving.
PSA.150.6: This final verse of the entire book of Psalms calls on every living, breathing thing to join in praise.
PRO.1.7: Near the start of the book, this proverb sets up fearing God as the starting point for actually knowing anything worthwhile.
PRO.3.5: Solomon, addressing this collection of sayings to 'my son,' tells him to trust God rather than lean only on his own reasoning.
PRO.3.6: The next line in the same proverb tells the reader that including God in every decision will keep their path straight.
PRO.4.23: In a father's advice to his son, this proverb singles out the heart as the thing most worth guarding closely.
PRO.10.12: One of Solomon's short, paired sayings, this proverb contrasts what hatred stirs up with what love is able to cover.
PRO.12.25: In this short proverb, Solomon notes how a heavy heart weighs a person down, but a kind word can lift it.
PRO.13.12: Among Solomon's proverbs about everyday life, this one names the ache of a delayed hope and the relief when what's wanted finally comes.
PRO.14.12: Solomon warns his readers in this collection of sayings that a path can feel completely right to a person and still end in death.
PRO.15.1: One of Solomon's proverbs about speech, this one contrasts a gentle reply with words that provoke anger.
PRO.16.3: Speaking as a father instructing his son, Solomon advises handing your plans over to God as the way to see them succeed.
PRO.16.9: In this collection of practical sayings, Solomon admits people plan their own course, but credits God with directing where their steps land.
PRO.16.18: One of Solomon's short warnings to his son, this saying cautions that overconfidence tends to come right before a fall.
PRO.17.17: Solomon, teaching his son about relationships, distinguishes a friend's constant loyalty from a brother's loyalty specifically in hard times.
PRO.17.22: Among his sayings about daily life, Solomon compares a cheerful outlook to medicine, and a crushed spirit to something that wears the body down.
PRO.18.10: Teaching his son to trust God for safety, Solomon here pictures God's name as a fortified tower the righteous can run into.
PRO.18.24: Solomon tells his son to be the kind of friend worth having, then points to a friend who sticks closer than a brother would.
PRO.19.21: In this collection of Solomon's sayings, many plans fill a person's mind, but only God's own plan is said to hold up.
PRO.22.6: This proverb offers a father's confidence that early training in a child's life will shape the direction of their adult life.
PRO.24.16: Solomon assures his son here that even a good person stumbles again and again, yet keeps getting back up each time.
PRO.27.17: Teaching his son about friendship, Solomon pictures two pieces of iron sharpening each other as what one friend can do for another.
PRO.28.13: Among sayings about honesty, Solomon contrasts hiding wrongdoing, which never works, with admitting it, which leads to mercy.
PRO.29.18: Solomon warns his son in this saying that people lose their way when they have no larger vision guiding them.
PRO.31.30: Near the close of a poem, part of what King Lemuel's mother taught him about a capable woman, this line says fearing God outlasts charm and beauty.
ECC.1.2: Writing as 'the Preacher,' a king in Jerusalem reflecting on his life, this opens the book by declaring everything he chased amounts to nothing lasting.
ECC.3.1: Writing as 'the Preacher' reflecting on the shape of life, the writer opens this list by saying every activity has its own proper time.
ECC.3.11: Continuing the same reflection on times and seasons, the Preacher says people sense something lasting beyond what they can fully grasp.
ECC.4.9: In the middle of reflecting on the emptiness of working alone, the Preacher points out that two people working together do better than one.
ECC.9.10: The Preacher, reflecting on how short life is, urges the reader to throw full effort into whatever they're doing while they're still alive.
ECC.12.13: This closes the entire book, with the Preacher summing up everything he has said in one final piece of advice.
SNG.6.3: In this love poem attributed to Solomon, the woman speaking affirms her mutual belonging with the man she loves.
SNG.8.7: Near the end of the same love poem, the woman describes love as something no flood or fortune could buy or destroy.
ISA.1.18: Confronting a nation that had kept up religious rituals while ignoring justice, God invites them through Isaiah to reason honestly with him.
ISA.2.4: In a vision about the future given to the prophet Isaiah, weapons of war are described being turned into farming tools.
ISA.6.8: After seeing a vision of God in the temple and having his own guilt dealt with, Isaiah hears God asking for someone to send, and volunteers.
ISA.7.14: Speaking to a frightened king named Ahaz, Isaiah gives a sign involving a coming child; Matthew's Gospel later applies this to the birth of Jesus.
ISA.9.6: In a passage about a future ruler bringing lasting peace, Isaiah names several titles this coming child will carry.
ISA.11.6: Describing a future age of peace under a coming ruler, Isaiah pictures natural enemies among animals living safely side by side.
ISA.12.2: This is a short song of thanks Isaiah gives the people to sing about a coming day when God's anger has passed.
ISA.26.3: Part of a song Isaiah gives Judah to sing, this verse describes steady peace for anyone whose mind stays fixed on God.
ISA.30.21: Speaking of a future time when the people finally listen to their teachers, Isaiah describes a voice guiding them which way to turn.
ISA.40.8: Opening a new section of comfort for a discouraged nation, Isaiah contrasts how quickly people fade with how permanent God's word is.
ISA.40.11: In the same passage of comfort, Isaiah pictures God tending his people gently, the way a shepherd carries young lambs.
ISA.40.29: Speaking to an exhausted, discouraged nation, Isaiah describes a God who gives strength to people who have none left.
ISA.40.31: This closes the same passage, promising that people who keep waiting on God will find their strength renewed.
ISA.41.10: Speaking to a fearful, exiled people, Isaiah delivers this reassurance from God not to be afraid, because God will hold them up.
ISA.43.1: Speaking to a people who felt abandoned, Isaiah delivers God's message that they still belong to him by name.
ISA.43.2: Continuing the same message, Isaiah describes God's presence with the people through danger, using water and fire as pictures.
ISA.43.19: In a message about restoration after hardship, Isaiah has God announce something new, like a road appearing through empty desert.
ISA.43.25: Speaking for God to a people who had grown distant, Isaiah delivers a promise that their wrongs will be forgotten, not held against them.
ISA.49.15: Isaiah compares God's care to something even stronger than a mother's bond with her nursing child.
ISA.49.16: Right after comparing God to a mother, Isaiah pictures the people themselves engraved permanently on the palms of God's own hands.
ISA.53.3: Describing a suffering servant figure rejected by those around him, Isaiah writes lines the New Testament later applies to Jesus.
ISA.53.4: Continuing the same description, Isaiah pictures this servant carrying suffering that wasn't originally his own.
ISA.53.5: Still describing the suffering servant, Isaiah connects this figure's wounds to healing for others, a passage Peter later quotes about Jesus.
ISA.53.6: This verse pictures people wandering like lost sheep, with their wrongdoing placed instead onto the suffering servant Isaiah describes.
ISA.54.17: In a passage of comfort after judgment, Isaiah promises that no weapon aimed at God's people will ultimately succeed.
ISA.55.8: Inviting people to turn back to God, Isaiah has God explain that his thinking works differently than human thinking does.
ISA.60.1: Opening a vision of future restoration for Jerusalem, Isaiah calls the city to rise because light has arrived.
ISA.64.8: Praying on behalf of a guilty nation, Isaiah pictures God as a potter shaping his people like clay.
ISA.66.13: Near the end of the book, Isaiah promises Jerusalem comfort like that of a mother comforting her child.
JER.1.5: At the start of his call to be a prophet, Jeremiah hears God say he was known and appointed before he was even born.
JER.17.7: In a passage contrasting two kinds of people, Jeremiah describes the one who trusts in God as genuinely fortunate.
JER.17.9: Right after describing the trusting person, Jeremiah adds this blunt warning about how easily the human heart deceives itself.
JER.29.11: Writing a letter to exiles settled in Babylon, Jeremiah passes along God's message that their future still holds hope.
JER.29.13: Continuing the same letter to the exiles, Jeremiah says that searching for God wholeheartedly is how they'll find him.
JER.31.3: In a message of restoration to exiled Israel, Jeremiah describes God's love for the nation as lasting and unbroken.
JER.33.3: Speaking to Jeremiah while he was imprisoned during the siege of Jerusalem, God invites him to call out and expect an answer.
LAM.3.22: Mourning the destruction of Jerusalem, the writer of Lamentations pauses to say that God's mercy is the reason anything remains.
LAM.3.23: Right after that admission, the same writer describes God's faithfulness as something renewed every single morning.
LAM.3.26: Still grieving the city's fall, the writer of Lamentations concludes that waiting quietly for God's rescue is the better path.
EZK.36.26: Speaking to exiles in Babylon, Ezekiel delivers God's promise of an inner change, replacing a hardened heart with a responsive one.
EZK.37.5: In a vision of a valley full of dry bones, Ezekiel hears God promise to breathe life back into them.
DAN.10.19: After a terrifying vision leaves Daniel weak and speechless, a heavenly messenger tells him not to be afraid and strengthens him.
HOS.6.6: Speaking to a nation going through the motions of worship, Hosea delivers God's preference for genuine care over empty ritual; Jesus later quotes this line.
HOS.14.4: Closing his book with a call to return to God, Hosea delivers a promise that God will heal Israel's wandering and love them freely.
JOL.2.25: After a locust plague had stripped the land bare, Joel delivers God's promise to restore what those years had eaten away.
AMO.5.24: Rejecting a nation's religious festivals while injustice continued, Amos calls instead for fairness to flow like a constant stream.
JON.2.2: Swallowed by a great fish after running from God, Jonah prays this line from inside its belly.
MIC.6.8: Answering the question of what sacrifice could possibly please God, Micah says God has already made it simple.
MIC.7.19: Closing his book with hope after chapters of warning, Micah pictures God throwing the nation's sins into the depths of the sea.
NAM.1.7: In a book largely about coming judgment on Nineveh, Nahum pauses to describe God as a safe place for anyone who trusts him.
HAB.1.2: Opening his book with a complaint, the prophet Habakkuk asks God how long he must cry out about violence before being heard.
HAB.3.19: Closing his book after wrestling with God over injustice, Habakkuk declares his strength in God even if the harvest completely fails.
ZEP.3.17: In a passage promising restoration for Jerusalem, Zephaniah describes God not just saving his people but delighting in them with singing.
ZEC.4.6: Giving Zerubbabel encouragement for rebuilding the temple, an angel delivers this message that the work depends on God's spirit, not on force.
MAT.4.4: Fasting alone in the wilderness, Jesus responds to the devil's suggestion that he turn stones into bread by quoting Deuteronomy.
MAT.5.3: This opens the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus sits down before a crowd on a hillside and begins teaching his disciples.
MAT.5.4: Continuing that same hillside teaching, Jesus names people who are grieving as among those who will be comforted.
MAT.5.5: Still in the same teaching, Jesus says people who don't push their way to the front will end up inheriting the earth.
MAT.5.6: Continuing the same list, Jesus describes people who are hungry for things to be made right as people who will be satisfied.
MAT.5.7: Further into the same teaching, Jesus connects showing mercy to others with receiving mercy in return.
MAT.5.8: Still teaching the crowd on the hillside, Jesus says people with undivided, honest hearts are the ones who will see God.
MAT.5.9: In this same hillside teaching known as the Beatitudes, Jesus calls people who make peace the ones who will be recognized as God's children.
MAT.5.14: Continuing the same hillside teaching, Jesus tells his listeners they are the light of the world, like a city set on a hill that cannot be hidden.
MAT.5.16: Right after the light comparison, Jesus tells the crowd why that light matters: so people notice good actions and credit God.
MAT.5.39: Addressing an old rule about fair payback, Jesus tells his listeners to respond to a slap by not retaliating at all.
MAT.6.9: Teaching his disciples how to pray, Jesus gives them this opening line as a model to follow.
MAT.6.11: Continuing the model prayer he gave his disciples, Jesus includes this simple request for each day's needs.
MAT.6.12: The same model prayer continues with a line linking being forgiven to forgiving others.
MAT.6.14: Right after teaching the model prayer, Jesus explains what happens when his listeners forgive other people.
MAT.6.21: In a teaching about where to put your effort, Jesus tells the crowd that their heart follows whatever they treasure.
MAT.6.26: Pointing to birds flying overhead, Jesus asks his listeners to notice how God feeds them without their working for it.
MAT.10.31: Sending his disciples out to preach, Jesus reassures them of their worth by comparing them to sparrows.
MAT.6.33: Still teaching about worry over food and clothing, Jesus tells the crowd what to prioritize instead.
MAT.6.34: Closing his teaching on worry, Jesus tells the crowd not to borrow trouble from a day that hasn't come yet.
MAT.7.1: In a teaching about how people treat each other, Jesus opens with a short warning against judging others.
MAT.7.7: Continuing to teach the crowd, Jesus encourages them to keep asking, searching, and knocking.
MAT.7.12: Summarizing a large section of his teaching, Jesus reduces it to one rule about treating others the way you want to be treated.
MAT.7.14: Describing two possible paths, Jesus tells the crowd that the one leading to life is narrow and less traveled.
MAT.7.24: Closing the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus compares someone who acts on his words to a builder who chose solid rock.
MAT.11.28: Speaking to a crowd worn down by life, Jesus invites anyone tired and burdened to come to him for rest.
MAT.11.29: Right after that invitation, Jesus describes himself as gentle and humble, offering rest to those who follow him.
MAT.14.31: After Peter starts walking on the water toward him and then panics and sinks, Jesus catches him and asks why he doubted.
MAT.17.20: After the disciples fail to heal a boy, Jesus tells them that faith as small as a mustard seed would have been enough.
MAT.18.20: Teaching about resolving conflict within a community, Jesus promises his own presence wherever even a small group gathers in his name.
MAT.19.6: Responding to a question about divorce, Jesus describes marriage as something God joins that people shouldn't split apart.
MAT.19.14: When his disciples try to keep children away from him, Jesus tells them to let the children come instead.
MAT.19.26: After his disciples wonder aloud who could possibly be saved, Jesus tells them that what's impossible for people isn't impossible for God.
MAT.22.37: Asked by a religious lawyer to name the most important commandment, Jesus answers with total love for God.
MAT.25.40: In a story about a king judging the nations, Jesus says that kindness shown to the overlooked counts as kindness shown to him.
MAT.28.6: At the empty tomb on the first Easter morning, an angel tells the frightened women that Jesus is not there because he has risen.
MAT.28.19: Meeting his disciples on a mountain after his resurrection, Jesus sends them out to teach and baptize people everywhere.
MAT.28.20: This closes Matthew's Gospel, with the risen Jesus promising his disciples his ongoing presence until the end of time.
MRK.1.17: Walking beside the sea and watching two fishermen at work, Jesus calls them to leave their nets and follow him instead.
MRK.4.39: Woken up during a violent storm on the lake, Jesus speaks directly to the wind and waves, and they go still.
MRK.4.40: Right after calming the storm, Jesus asks his frightened disciples why they still had no faith.
MRK.5.36: Just after hearing that a synagogue leader's daughter has died, Jesus tells the grieving father not to be afraid, only to believe.
MRK.8.36: Teaching his disciples about the cost of following him, Jesus asks what good it does to gain everything and lose yourself.
MRK.9.24: Asked by Jesus whether he believes healing is possible, a desperate father cries out this honest, mixed admission.
MRK.11.24: Teaching his disciples about prayer after a fig tree withers, Jesus tells them to pray with real expectation of receiving.
LUK.2.10: Appearing to shepherds watching their flocks at night, an angel tells them not to be afraid, bringing news of great joy.
LUK.2.11: Right after telling the shepherds not to be afraid, the angel announces that a savior has been born in Bethlehem.
LUK.2.14: Following the angel's announcement to the shepherds, a whole host of angels bursts into praise over the newborn child.
LUK.6.35: Teaching a crowd about loving enemies, Jesus tells them to do good and lend without expecting anything back.
LUK.6.38: Continuing to teach about generosity, Jesus tells the crowd that what they give will come back to them in full measure.
LUK.9.23: After Peter recognizes him as the Messiah, Jesus tells his disciples what following him will actually require of them daily.
LUK.12.7: Reassuring his followers not to fear those who could harm them, Jesus points out that even their hairs are counted.
LUK.15.7: Ending a short story about a shepherd finding one lost sheep, Jesus describes the joy in heaven over one person who changes course.
LUK.15.20: In a story about a runaway son who finally heads home, Jesus describes the father spotting him from far off and running to meet him.
LUK.15.24: Still telling the same story, Jesus has the father explain the celebration: a son thought dead has come back alive.
LUK.19.10: After spending time in the home of Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector, Jesus explains why he came to a man his neighbors despised.
LUK.22.42: Praying alone on the Mount of Olives hours before his arrest, Jesus asks to be spared what's coming, but yields to God's will.
LUK.23.34: Nailed to the cross between two criminals, Jesus asks God to forgive the people carrying out his execution.
JHN.1.1: Opening his account of Jesus with poetic language rather than a birth story, John identifies Jesus as 'the Word,' present with God from the very beginning.
JHN.1.5: Continuing that same opening poem, John describes light entering the dark world and the darkness failing to overcome it.
JHN.1.12: Still in his prologue, John explains what happens to anyone who actually receives and trusts this Word made known as Jesus.
JHN.1.14: John closes his opening poem by describing this eternal Word becoming human and living among ordinary people.
JHN.3.16: Talking at night with Nicodemus, a religious leader who came to him secretly, Jesus explains why God sent his son into the world.
JHN.3.17: Continuing the same nighttime conversation, Jesus clarifies that his purpose was rescue, not condemnation.
JHN.6.35: After feeding a huge crowd with a few loaves of bread, Jesus tells them the next day that he himself is what truly satisfies.
JHN.8.7: When religious leaders bring a woman caught in adultery to test him, Jesus responds with a challenge about who is qualified to throw the first stone.
JHN.8.12: Still teaching in the temple after that encounter, Jesus tells the crowd that following him means walking out of darkness.
JHN.8.32: Speaking to Jews who had just begun to trust him, Jesus links staying faithful to his teaching with actually being set free.
JHN.10.10: Describing his purpose using the image of a shepherd and thieves, Jesus contrasts destruction with the full life he came to give.
JHN.10.11: Continuing the shepherd imagery, Jesus describes himself as the shepherd willing to die for the sheep in his care.
JHN.11.25: Speaking to Martha, whose brother Lazarus had just died, Jesus tells her that life and resurrection are found in him personally.
JHN.11.35: Standing at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, surrounded by mourners, Jesus is described in this shortest verse simply weeping.
JHN.13.34: During his last meal with his disciples, right after washing their feet, Jesus gives them a new instruction about loving one another.
JHN.13.35: Right after giving that instruction, Jesus tells his disciples that love for each other is what will identify them to others.
JHN.14.1: Still at the same last meal, sensing his disciples' fear about what's coming, Jesus tells them not to let their hearts be troubled.
JHN.14.2: Continuing to comfort his disciples before his death, Jesus describes going ahead to prepare a place for them.
JHN.14.6: Answering Thomas's question about how to know the way to the Father, Jesus identifies himself as that way.
JHN.14.18: Still preparing his disciples for his departure, Jesus promises he won't leave them permanently alone.
JHN.14.27: Continuing his farewell to his disciples, Jesus leaves them a kind of peace he says is different from what the world offers.
JHN.15.5: Using a vineyard as a picture, Jesus describes himself as the vine and his followers as branches that depend entirely on him.
JHN.15.13: Still speaking at the same last meal, Jesus defines the greatest possible love as laying down one's life for friends.
JHN.16.22: Warning his disciples that grief is coming before he leaves them, Jesus promises a joy afterward that no one will be able to take away.
JHN.16.33: Closing this same farewell conversation, Jesus tells his disciples to expect trouble in the world but take heart because he has already overcome it.
JHN.19.30: Dying on the cross after being given a final drink, Jesus speaks three words before he dies.
JHN.20.27: Appearing to his disciples eight days after his resurrection, Jesus invites the doubting Thomas to touch his wounds directly.
JHN.20.29: Right after Thomas finally believes upon seeing him, Jesus adds a blessing for people who will believe without ever seeing him at all.
ACT.1.8: Just before ascending into the sky, Jesus tells his gathered followers what will happen once the promised Spirit comes upon them.
ACT.2.38: After a crowd is cut to the heart by his sermon and asks what to do, Peter answers with instructions about repentance and baptism.
ACT.3.6: Meeting a man who had been unable to walk his whole life, begging at the temple gate, Peter offers him something other than money.
ACT.4.12: Standing before the Jewish council that had arrested him, Peter insists that the name of Jesus is the only one that can rescue anyone.
ACT.16.31: After an earthquake breaks open his prison, a terrified jailer asks Paul and Silas what he must do; this is their answer.
ACT.17.28: Speaking to Greek philosophers in Athens, Paul makes his point by quoting their own poets back to them.
ACT.20.35: Saying goodbye to leaders of the Ephesian church he doesn't expect to see again, Paul reminds them of something Jesus once said about giving.
ROM.1.16: Introducing himself to a church he had never visited, Paul explains in this letter why he isn't embarrassed to preach about Jesus.
ROM.5.1: Early in this letter to the Roman church, Paul describes the peace with God that comes through trusting Jesus.
ROM.5.8: Making his case for God's love, Paul points out that Jesus died for people while they were still doing wrong.
ROM.6.23: Contrasting two different endings, Paul describes what sin earns against what God gives freely instead.
ROM.8.1: Opening a chapter about life empowered by God's Spirit, Paul assures believers in Jesus that they are no longer condemned.
ROM.8.16: Continuing to describe life in the Spirit, Paul says that same Spirit confirms to believers that they belong to God's family.
ROM.8.18: Comparing present difficulty to future glory, Paul argues that current suffering doesn't measure up to what's coming.
ROM.8.26: Still writing about the Spirit's help, Paul describes the Spirit praying on believers' behalf when they don't know what to say.
ROM.8.28: Reassuring a church facing hardship, Paul writes that God works everything together for good for those who love him.
ROM.8.31: Building toward the climax of this chapter, Paul asks a rhetorical question about who could possibly stand against people God is for.
ROM.8.37: Listing off threats like hardship and danger, Paul concludes that none of it can defeat people loved by God.
ROM.8.39: Closing this chapter, Paul declares that nothing in creation can cut believers off from God's love found in Jesus.
ROM.10.9: Explaining what it means to trust in Jesus, Paul ties together an honest confession with a genuine belief in the resurrection.
ROM.10.13: Continuing that same explanation, Paul writes that calling on the name of the Lord is open to anyone at all.
ROM.12.2: Urging the Roman church to live differently from the culture around them, Paul calls for a change starting with how they think.
ROM.12.15: In a list of practical instructions for community life, Paul tells believers to share fully in both celebration and grief.
ROM.12.21: Closing a passage about responding to enemies without revenge, Paul sums it up as overcoming evil by doing good instead.
ROM.13.10: Discussing how believers should treat each other, Paul reduces a list of commandments down to a single principle about love.
ROM.15.13: Near the close of his letter, Paul prays that the Roman believers would be filled with joy, peace, and hope.
1CO.2.9: Writing to a divided church in Corinth about wisdom beyond human understanding, Paul quotes a line about things no one has ever seen or imagined.
1CO.6.19: Confronting sexual immorality within the Corinthian church, Paul reminds them that their own bodies now house God's Spirit.
1CO.9.24: Using the image of a foot race, Paul urges the Corinthian believers to run their own lives with the same focus as an athlete chasing a prize.
1CO.10.13: Warning the Corinthians against repeating Israel's past mistakes, Paul reassures them that God limits how much hardship they'll face at once.
1CO.13.1: Opening his famous chapter on love, Paul says that even the most impressive spiritual gifts amount to noise without it.
1CO.13.8: Continuing that same chapter, Paul contrasts love's permanence with the temporary nature of spiritual gifts like prophecy.
1CO.13.11: Still writing about love, Paul compares his own growth from childhood to adulthood as a picture of partial knowledge becoming complete.
1CO.13.12: Near the end of the same chapter, Paul admits that present understanding is like a blurry reflection compared to what's coming.
1CO.13.13: This closes the chapter on love, with Paul ranking faith, hope, and love together, but naming love as the greatest.
1CO.15.55: In a chapter defending the resurrection, Paul taunts death itself, asking where its power has gone.
1CO.15.57: Right after taunting death, Paul thanks God for the victory Jesus provides.
2CO.1.4: Opening this letter to a church he'd had a painful history with, Paul explains that God comforts him precisely so he can comfort others.
2CO.4.16: Describing the physical toll of his ministry, Paul contrasts his outward decline with an inward renewal happening at the same time.
2CO.4.18: Continuing that same thought, Paul tells the Corinthians to focus on what can't be seen rather than what's only temporary.
2CO.5.7: Explaining how he lives with uncertainty about the future, Paul says his confidence rests on trust rather than on visible proof.
2CO.5.17: Describing what changes when someone commits to Christ, Paul says the old identity is gone and something new has begun.
2CO.9.7: Encouraging the Corinthians to follow through on a promised gift for a struggling church, Paul says God loves a giver who gives gladly.
2CO.12.9: After begging God three times to remove a painful affliction, Paul reports the answer he received about God's strength working through weakness.
GAL.2.20: Defending his gospel of grace to churches being pressured toward old religious rules, Paul describes his old identity as replaced by Christ living in him.
GAL.3.28: Arguing that faith in Christ erases old social divisions, Paul lists ethnicity, status, and gender as no longer determining anyone's standing.
GAL.4.7: Explaining what changes for a believer, Paul contrasts being a slave with being an heir who receives an inheritance.
GAL.6.2: Instructing the Galatian churches on caring for each other, Paul tells them to help carry what weighs each other down.
GAL.6.9: Encouraging believers who feel worn out doing good, Paul promises a harvest will come if they don't quit.
EPH.2.8: Writing likely from prison to a church in Ephesus, Paul explains that their rescue came as a gift, not something they earned.
EPH.2.10: Right after describing their rescue as a gift, Paul adds that believers are shaped by God to do good things he already planned.
EPH.4.32: Instructing the Ephesian church on how to treat each other, Paul ties their forgiveness of one another to the forgiveness they've received.
EPH.6.10: Opening a passage about spiritual struggle, Paul tells the Ephesian believers to draw their strength from God rather than themselves.
EPH.6.11: Continuing the same passage, Paul tells believers to dress in spiritual armor to stand against opposition.
PHP.1.6: Writing warmly to a church that had supported him financially, Paul expresses confidence that the good work started in them will be finished.
PHP.2.3: Urging unity within the Philippian church, Paul tells them to consider others as more important than themselves.
PHP.3.14: Describing his own spiritual pursuit as an ongoing race, Paul says he keeps pressing toward the goal rather than settling.
PHP.4.4: Writing from prison to a church that had sent him support, Paul repeats a simple command to rejoice.
PHP.4.6: Continuing that same letter, Paul tells the Philippians to bring their worries to God in prayer instead of carrying them alone.
PHP.4.7: Right after that instruction about prayer, Paul describes a peace that goes beyond ordinary understanding.
PHP.4.8: Closing his practical instructions, Paul gives the Philippians a list of the kinds of things worth thinking about.
PHP.4.11: Thanking the Philippians for a gift while writing from prison, Paul says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances.
PHP.4.13: Continuing to describe his contentment, Paul credits his ability to handle any situation to the strength Christ provides.
PHP.4.19: Closing his thanks for their gift, Paul assures the Philippians that God will take care of whatever they need in return.
COL.1.17: Describing who Jesus is to a church facing false teaching, Paul says everything holds together because of him.
COL.3.2: Encouraging the Colossian church toward a new focus, Paul tells them to set their minds on things above rather than earthly concerns.
COL.3.13: Instructing the Colossian church on relationships, Paul ties forgiving each other directly to how Christ forgave them.
COL.3.15: Continuing the same instructions, Paul tells the Colossians to let God's peace govern how they treat each other.
COL.3.17: Closing a section on everyday conduct, Paul tells the Colossians to do everything they say or do in Jesus's name.
1TH.4.13: Comforting a church worried about believers who had already died, Paul writes to correct their grief with genuine hope.
1TH.4.14: Continuing that same comfort, Paul ties the resurrection of Jesus directly to the hope for those who have died trusting him.
1TH.5.17: In a rapid list of short instructions closing his letter, Paul tells the Thessalonians to keep praying without stopping.
1TH.5.18: Right after that instruction, Paul tells the Thessalonians to give thanks in every situation, not just good ones.
2TH.3.3: Reassuring a church worried about difficult people around them, Paul says God is faithful to strengthen and protect them.
2TH.3.16: Closing his second letter to the Thessalonians, Paul prays for the Lord's peace to be with them at all times.
1TI.4.12: Writing to Timothy, a younger coworker facing skepticism because of his age, Paul tells him to lead by example instead.
1TI.6.6: Warning against teachers who treat religion as a way to get rich, Paul redefines real gain as contentment with what you have.
1TI.6.10: Continuing that same warning, Paul identifies the love of money, not money itself, as the root of many troubles.
2TI.1.7: Writing to encourage Timothy, Paul reminds him that God gives believers power, love, and self-control, not a spirit of fear.
2TI.2.15: Instructing Timothy on handling his responsibilities well, Paul tells him to work hard at rightly explaining the truth.
2TI.3.16: Explaining the value of Scripture to Timothy, Paul says it's useful for teaching, correcting, and training people to live well.
2TI.4.7: Writing near the end of his life, likely awaiting execution, Paul tells Timothy he has fought his fight and stayed faithful to the end.
HEB.4.12: Written to Jewish believers tempted to abandon their faith, this letter describes God's word as sharp enough to reach into a person's deepest thoughts.
HEB.4.16: Continuing the same argument, the writer encourages believers to approach God's throne boldly rather than fearfully.
HEB.11.1: Opening a long chapter listing examples of trust from Israel's history, the writer defines what that kind of trust actually is.
HEB.11.6: Still in the same chapter about historical examples of trust, the writer says pleasing God starts with believing he exists and rewards those who seek him.
HEB.12.2: Comparing the life of faith to a long-distance race, the writer tells readers to keep their attention on Jesus, who endured the cross for what was ahead of him.
HEB.13.5: Warning against greed near the end of the letter, the writer reminds readers of a promise that God will never abandon them.
HEB.13.8: This short verse closes a section about steady leaders by describing Jesus himself as never changing over time.
JAS.1.5: Writing to Jewish believers scattered outside their homeland, James tells them that anyone lacking wisdom can simply ask God for it.
JAS.1.6: Right after that promise, James adds a condition: ask with genuine trust, not the back-and-forth of someone unsure.
JAS.1.12: Encouraging readers going through hard testing, James promises a lasting reward to those who stay faithful through it.
JAS.1.17: Describing where good things ultimately come from, James calls every good gift a gift that comes down from God, who never changes.
JAS.1.19: Giving practical advice for everyday relationships, James tells his readers to be quick to listen and slow to speak or get angry.
JAS.2.17: Arguing that real trust shows up in action, James says trust with no accompanying action is essentially lifeless.
JAS.4.8: Calling his readers back to sincerity, James tells them that drawing near to God results in God drawing near to them.
JAS.5.16: Instructing a community on prayer and honesty, James tells readers to admit their wrongs to each other and pray for one another.
1PE.2.9: Writing to Christians scattered across the empire and facing suspicion, Peter tells them they belong to a people specially called out of darkness.
1PE.3.15: Advising Christians facing hostility for their faith, Peter tells them to be ready to explain their hope calmly, without hostility in return.
1PE.4.8: Near the end of his letter, Peter tells a persecuted church that love toward each other should come before anything else.
1PE.5.6: Instructing a church under pressure, Peter tells them to humble themselves under God rather than trying to control their own outcome.
1PE.5.7: Right after that instruction, Peter tells readers to hand over their anxiety to God because he genuinely cares about them.
1PE.5.8: Closing his letter with a warning, Peter compares the devil to a roaring lion looking for someone to attack.
2PE.3.9: Responding to people mocking the idea that Jesus would ever return, Peter explains God's delay as patience, giving people time to change.
1JN.1.9: Writing against a teaching that denied the reality of wrongdoing, John tells readers that admitting it leads to being forgiven and made clean.
1JN.3.1: Marveling at what it means to be part of God's family, John tells his readers to notice the kind of love the Father has given them.
1JN.3.2: Continuing that same thought, John admits that what believers will eventually become isn't fully clear yet.
1JN.3.18: Warning against love that's just talk, John tells his readers that real love shows up in action, not only words.
1JN.4.8: Making a direct statement about God's character, John says anyone who doesn't love doesn't actually know God, because God himself is love.
1JN.4.18: Continuing to write about love, John says genuine love pushes out fear rather than existing alongside it.
1JN.4.19: Right after that thought, John gives the reason people are even capable of loving: God loved them first.
1JN.5.14: Closing his letter with confidence about prayer, John says believers can be sure God hears requests that line up with his will.
REV.1.8: Opening this vision given to John while exiled on the island of Patmos, the Lord identifies himself as the beginning and the end of everything.
REV.2.10: In a message to a persecuted church in the city of Smyrna, Jesus tells them not to fear coming suffering and promises them life.
REV.3.20: In a message to a self-satisfied church in Laodicea, Jesus pictures himself standing outside, knocking, waiting to be let in.
REV.21.4: Describing a vision of a renewed heaven and earth, John writes that God will personally wipe away every tear and end death itself.
REV.21.5: Right after that vision, the one seated on the throne speaks directly, announcing that he is making everything new.
ISA.43.4: Speaking to a people facing exile and defeat, Isaiah delivers God's message that they are precious and deeply valued to him.
PSA.107.8: Recalling how God rescued people who cried out to him in distress, this psalm calls on them to actually thank him for it.
PSA.34.4: Written after David escaped a dangerous situation by pretending to be insane, this verse recalls him seeking God and finding relief from fear.
1CO.15.58: Closing his long chapter on the resurrection, Paul tells the Corinthians that their efforts for God are never ultimately wasted.
MAT.6.24: Teaching the crowd on a hillside, Jesus warns that trying to serve both God and money will pull a person apart.
GEN.8.22: After the flood, God makes this promise to himself following Noah's sacrifice, assuring the seasons will keep coming.
PRO.4.7: In this fatherly advice to his son, Solomon urges that gaining wisdom matters more than anything else a person could get.
LUK.16.10: Concluding a parable about a dishonest manager, Jesus tells his disciples that handling small things well reveals how they'll handle much.
GEN.28.16: After dreaming of a ladder reaching to heaven, Jacob wakes up and realizes God was present in that ordinary place all along.
EXO.4.12: When Moses protests that he isn't a good speaker, God tells him at the burning bush that he will help him find the words.
EXO.20.8: One of the Ten Commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai, this one tells the people to set the seventh day apart as holy.
DEU.7.6: Moses tells the people of Israel, as they prepare to enter the promised land, that God has set them apart as his own.
JAS.1.27: Writing to scattered believers, James defines genuine faith not as ritual but as caring for orphans and widows in need.
EXO.20.17: The last of the Ten Commandments Moses received on Sinai addresses wanting what already belongs to a neighbor.
JHN.15.15: At the last supper, Jesus tells his disciples he no longer calls them servants but friends he has told everything to.
DEU.32.4: Near the end of his life, Moses recites this song to Israel, calling God a faithful Rock whose ways are always right.
JOS.1.8: After Moses dies, God instructs Joshua, the new leader, to keep the book of the law close and obey it constantly.
RUT.2.12: In his field, Boaz blesses Ruth, a foreign widow gleaning grain, for the loyalty she has shown her mother-in-law.
ROM.8.35: Paul asks the Roman church a question, listing hardships like hunger and danger that still can't sever Christ's love.
1SA.12.24: In his farewell speech as Israel's leader, Samuel urges the people to serve God faithfully, remembering all he has done.
1SA.17.45: Facing the giant Goliath on the battlefield, young David answers his taunts by naming the God he's fighting for.
2SA.12.13: After the prophet Nathan confronts him over his sin with Bathsheba, David confesses, and Nathan tells him he's forgiven.
1KI.3.9: Newly crowned king, Solomon asks God in a dream at Gibeon for a wise and understanding heart to govern the people well.
JHN.6.68: After many disciples desert Jesus over a hard teaching, Peter tells him there's nowhere else worth going.
2KI.20.5: When King Hezekiah becomes deathly ill and prays, God sends Isaiah back to say his tears have been seen and he'll be healed.
ISA.45.15: In an oracle about God's plans for the nations, Isaiah pauses to admit that Israel's God often works in hidden ways.
EST.4.16: Esther, a Jewish queen who must risk her life to approach the king unsummoned, asks her people to fast for her first.
JOB.12.12: Responding to his friends' arguments, Job points out that wisdom is usually expected to come with age and long experience.
JOB.33.4: A younger man named Elihu, breaking into Job's debate with his friends, insists that God's own breath gave him life.
JOB.42.2: After God speaks to him out of a whirlwind, Job replies humbly, admitting that nothing is beyond God's power.
JOB.42.10: Once Job prays for the friends who had accused him, God restores his fortunes, giving him twice what he had before.
PSA.3.3: Fleeing from his own son Absalom's rebellion, David writes this psalm calling God his shield and the one who lifts his head.
PSA.77.19: Remembering how God led Israel through the sea out of Egypt, this psalm marvels that God's paths remain beyond tracing.
PSA.19.7: In a psalm praising creation and God's instructions together, David says God's law can restore and renew a person's life.
PSA.126.3: Recalling Israel's return from exile, this song of ascents rejoices over what God has done for his people.
PSA.24.1: Opening a psalm about who may enter God's presence, David declares that the whole earth and everyone in it belongs to God.
PSA.25.7: David asks God in prayer to forget the sins and mistakes of his younger years, and to remember him instead with mercy.
PSA.27.10: In a psalm about trusting God amid enemies, David says even if his own parents abandoned him, God would take him in.
PSA.37.7: In this wisdom psalm, David tells his listener to stay calm and not be troubled when people who do wrong seem to prosper anyway.
PSA.145.16: In this same praise psalm, David marvels that God provides for the needs of every living creature, not just people.
PSA.40.2: David describes being lifted by God out of a pit of mud and set safely on solid rock after waiting patiently for rescue.
PSA.42.1: Dedicated to the sons of Korah, this psalm compares a deer's thirst for water to the writer's own deep longing for God.
PSA.116.7: Recalling a time he was brought low, the psalmist tells his own soul to rest again because God has been good to him.
PSA.131.2: David compares his own quieted, humble heart before God to a small child who has been weaned and calmed on its mother.
PRO.16.7: In this advice to his son, Solomon says that when a person's life pleases God, even enemies can end up at peace with them.
PSA.31.15: Surrounded by people plotting against him, David tells God in prayer that his times and future are held in God's hand.
PSA.55.17: Under pressure from enemies, David describes praying to God morning, noon, and night, confident he'll be heard.
PRO.17.14: Teaching his son how to handle conflict, Solomon warns him to walk away from a quarrel before it escalates beyond control.
PSA.62.8: David urges his listeners to trust God constantly and pour out their hearts to him, since God is a safe refuge for anyone.
PSA.68.5: In a psalm celebrating God's power on Israel's behalf, David highlights God's special concern for society's most vulnerable people.
PSA.71.9: Reflecting on a lifetime of trusting God since his youth, the psalmist prays for continued closeness now that he's grown old and weaker.
PSA.85.10: In a psalm hoping for Israel's restoration after judgment, the writer looks forward to God's mercy and justice finally working in harmony.
PSA.89.1: Written by a wise man named Ethan, this psalm opens with a vow to sing about God's faithful love for every generation.
PSA.90.1: In a prayer attributed to Moses, he calls God the home his people have always lived within, generation after generation.
PSA.94.19: Amid a flood of anxious thoughts, the psalmist admits it's God's comfort that brings his soul relief in this psalm about injustice.
PSA.100.3: In a short psalm calling every nation to worship, the writer reminds Israel that God made them and they belong to him.
PSA.103.13: In this psalm of praise, David compares God's compassion for those who fear him to a father's tenderness toward his children.
PSA.103.14: Continuing the same psalm, David explains why God treats people gently: he remembers that they're only dust.
PSA.104.24: Surveying the wonders of creation, the psalmist marvels at how wisely God made everything, filling the earth with riches.
PSA.112.7: Describing someone who lives in awe of God, this psalm says such a person can face bad news without being shaken by fear.
PRO.15.17: Teaching his son what really makes a home happy, Solomon weighs a loving family meal against wealth eaten amid conflict.
PSA.118.8: In a psalm of thanksgiving, the writer declares that trusting God offers more security than relying on people.
PSA.119.11: In the longest psalm in the Bible, the writer describes hiding God's word in his heart on purpose, so he won't sin against him.
PRO.27.6: Teaching his son to value honest friendship, Solomon warns that a flatterer's praise is more dangerous than a friend's hard truth.
1JN.4.11: Writing to believers about God's love shown through Jesus, John argues that such love obligates them to love each other too.
PSA.127.1: In a song of ascents credited to Solomon, the writer says that without God's own involvement, human effort at building or guarding falls apart.
PSA.130.1: This companion song of ascents pictures the writer calling out to God from what he names 'the depths,' an image of overwhelming trouble.
ECC.5.12: Weighing the downsides of wealth, the Preacher observes that a laborer sleeps soundly, while a rich man's abundance keeps him tossing awake.
PSA.139.17: In a psalm marveling at how completely God knows him, David says God's thoughts toward him outnumber anything he could count.
PSA.142.4: Hiding in a cave from Saul, David writes this psalm admitting that no one nearby seems to notice him or care for his safety.
PSA.143.8: Early in this prayer during a time of distress, David asks God to let him hear of his love each morning and show him which way to walk.
PSA.145.14: In this praise psalm, David points out that God notices the weak and struggling, not only the strong and successful.
PSA.147.4: Celebrating Jerusalem's restoration in this psalm, the writer marvels that the same God who heals broken hearts also names every star.
PRO.6.6: Addressing a sluggard directly, Solomon points him to the ant, urging him to learn diligence by watching how it works.
PRO.11.13: Solomon warns his son in this proverb that a gossip spreads secrets, while someone trustworthy keeps a confidence.
ROM.15.7: Near the end of a section on unity, Paul tells the Roman church to welcome each other the same way Christ welcomed them.
PRO.13.20: Solomon tells his son in this proverb that the company he keeps, wise or foolish, will end up shaping who he becomes.
PRO.21.21: In this collection of Solomon's own proverbs, chasing after goodness and mercy is said to bring life and honor.
PRO.15.22: Among his practical sayings, Solomon observes that plans collapse without advice, but succeed once many advisers weigh in.
PRO.16.24: Teaching his son about the power of words, Solomon compares kind speech to honey, sweet to the taste and good for the body.
PRO.16.32: Teaching his son the value of self-control, Solomon says mastering your own temper matters more than any military victory.
PRO.18.21: Solomon warns his son here that words carry real power, able to give life or bring harm, with the effects landing back on the speaker.
EPH.4.25: Instructing the Ephesian church on their new way of life, Paul tells them to stop lying and speak truthfully to each other instead.
PRO.19.17: Solomon tells his son that showing kindness to the poor is like making a loan directly to the Lord, who repays it in full.
PRO.20.1: Warning his son about habits that ruin good judgment, Solomon cautions him against being led astray by strong drink.
PRO.22.1: Teaching his son what to value most in life, Solomon ranks a trustworthy reputation above any amount of money.
PRO.25.21: Teaching his son how to treat an enemy, Solomon instructs him to feed a hungry rival and give a thirsty one water.
PRO.27.1: Solomon cautions his son against boasting about tomorrow, since no one actually knows what a single day will bring.
PRO.27.9: Teaching his son what good friendship looks like, Solomon commends a friend's heartfelt advice as one of life's true pleasures.
PRO.28.1: In a section contrasting the wicked and the righteous, Solomon tells his son how a guilty conscience can make a person fearful.
